feature: Put a copy back on its original's opacity
summary: Pick a copy of a component and the panel now has an Appearance section with an Opacity row, the same one every other layer gets. Fade the copy and a small back arrow appears next to the word Opacity; press it and the copy follows the original's opacity again. The same gap was hiding the Opacity row on an unlocked picture, so a screenshot can now be faded too.
setup: Photonz Dev, Experiments window, release Next. No flags to change: this is on by default.

try.do: Open the Library shelf and drag a Card component onto the canvas.
Click the copy you just placed.
Look at the Appearance section: it should have an Opacity row.
Drag the Opacity slider down to about a third.
Press the small back arrow that appeared next to the word Opacity.
Open a screenshot, unlock the Background layer, click it, and drag its Opacity down.

evaluate: Is the back arrow next to Opacity where you looked for it, or did you go hunting in the Component section instead?
Two ways back are on screen at once for a faded copy: the arrow on the Opacity row and the one on the Component section's Its own look row. Is that reassuring or is it clutter?
For a copy of a component the Appearance section holds only Opacity and Corner Radius. Does a section that short earn its heading, or should Opacity sit somewhere else for these layers?
After you press the back arrow, the Stopped following message is often still on screen even though the copy is following again. Did that confuse you?
Being able to fade a screenshot: is that something you wanted, and is Appearance where you would have gone for it?
rough: Pressing the back arrow says nothing at all, on purpose, so the Stopped following toast raised by the fade a moment earlier can still be on screen while the copy is following again. The message is not wrong when it appears, it just outlives the thing it describes. I left it alone rather than invent a Following again message nobody asked for.

The task described this as a component problem. It was wider: the Appearance section was shown only when a picked layer had a colour to paint, and Opacity leads that section, so anything that paints nothing of its own lost its opacity entirely. A copy of a component was one case, an unlocked picture was the other, which matters more given screenshots are the main material here. A plain group turned out to be fine, because picking one reaches the shapes inside it.
Screenshots here are real window captures, not offscreen renders: the probe had the Screen Recording grant.
